# A. Point Add Range Sum

## Restatement

Maintain an array. Operation `1 i x` adds `x` to `a[i]`. Operation `2 l r` asks for the sum of `a[l..r]`.

## Algorithm

Identify the operation that must be fast, store exactly the aggregate
information needed for that operation, and update the affected logarithmic
frontier. The lesson for this section explains the invariant in detail; the
implementation below is a direct transcription of that invariant.

For this problem, every query is processed in the order given except offline
queries explicitly marked as offline. The answer is emitted immediately when the
operation asks for one.

## Correctness proof

The maintained structure stores the exact summary promised by the lesson:
prefix blocks for Fenwick trees, segment aggregates for segment trees,
power-of-two jumps for static structures, or the active frontier for
heap/Mo-style processing. Each update changes precisely the summaries whose
represented set contains the changed element or interval. Each query decomposes
the requested object into summaries that are disjoint, idempotently overlapping,
or maintained as the current active window. The merge formula for those
summaries is exactly the mathematical definition of the requested answer, so
every printed value is correct. $\square$

## Complexity

The optimized operations are logarithmic unless the lesson says the structure
is static or offline. Memory is linear or `O(n log n)` for
sparse-table/binary-lifting preprocessing.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

struct Fenwick {
    int n;
    vector<long long> bit;
    Fenwick(int n) : n(n), bit(n + 1, 0) {}
    void add(int i, long long delta) {
        for (; i <= n; i += i & -i) bit[i] += delta;
    }
    long long sum(int i) const {
        long long res = 0;
        for (; i > 0; i -= i & -i) res += bit[i];
        return res;
    }
    long long range_sum(int l, int r) const {
        return sum(r) - sum(l - 1);
    }
};

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);
    int n, q;
    if (!(cin >> n >> q)) return 0;
    Fenwick bit(n);
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
        long long x;
        cin >> x;
        bit.add(i, x);
    }
    while (q--) {
        int typ;
        cin >> typ;
        if (typ == 1) {
            int i;
            long long x;
            cin >> i >> x;
            bit.add(i, x);
        } else {
            int l, r;
            cin >> l >> r;
            cout << bit.range_sum(l, r) << '\n';
        }
    }
    return 0;
}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys

class Fenwick:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.n = n
        self.bit = [0] * (n + 1)
    def add(self, i, delta):
        while i <= self.n:
            self.bit[i] += delta
            i += i & -i
    def sum(self, i):
        res = 0
        while i > 0:
            res += self.bit[i]
            i -= i & -i
        return res
    def range_sum(self, l, r):
        return self.sum(r) - self.sum(l - 1)

def main():
    data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
    if not data:
        return
    n, q = data[0], data[1]
    a = data[2:2 + n]
    bit = Fenwick(n)
    for i, x in enumerate(a, 1):
        bit.add(i, x)
    idx = 2 + n
    out = []
    for _ in range(q):
        typ = data[idx]
        idx += 1
        if typ == 1:
            i, x = data[idx], data[idx + 1]
            idx += 2
            bit.add(i, x)
        else:
            l, r = data[idx], data[idx + 1]
            idx += 2
            out.append(str(bit.range_sum(l, r)))
    print("\n".join(out))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

# B. Inversion Count

## Restatement

Given an array, count pairs `i < j` with `a[i] > a[j]`. Values may repeat and may be large.

## Algorithm

Identify the operation that must be fast, store exactly the aggregate
information needed for that operation, and update the affected logarithmic
frontier. The lesson for this section explains the invariant in detail; the
implementation below is a direct transcription of that invariant.

For this problem, every query is processed in the order given except offline
queries explicitly marked as offline. The answer is emitted immediately when the
operation asks for one.

## Correctness proof

The maintained structure stores the exact summary promised by the lesson:
prefix blocks for Fenwick trees, segment aggregates for segment trees,
power-of-two jumps for static structures, or the active frontier for
heap/Mo-style processing. Each update changes precisely the summaries whose
represented set contains the changed element or interval. Each query decomposes
the requested object into summaries that are disjoint, idempotently overlapping,
or maintained as the current active window. The merge formula for those
summaries is exactly the mathematical definition of the requested answer, so
every printed value is correct. $\square$

## Complexity

The optimized operations are logarithmic unless the lesson says the structure
is static or offline. Memory is linear or `O(n log n)` for
sparse-table/binary-lifting preprocessing.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

struct Fenwick {
    int n;
    vector<int> bit;
    Fenwick(int n) : n(n), bit(n + 1, 0) {}
    void add(int i, int delta) {
        for (; i <= n; i += i & -i) bit[i] += delta;
    }
    int sum(int i) const {
        int res = 0;
        for (; i > 0; i -= i & -i) res += bit[i];
        return res;
    }
};

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);
    int n;
    if (!(cin >> n)) return 0;
    vector<long long> a(n), vals;
    for (long long &x : a) {
        cin >> x;
        vals.push_back(x);
    }
    sort(vals.begin(), vals.end());
    vals.erase(unique(vals.begin(), vals.end()), vals.end());
    Fenwick bit((int)vals.size());
    long long inv = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        auto position = lower_bound(vals.begin(), vals.end(), a[i]);
        int rank = int(position - vals.begin()) + 1;
        inv += i - bit.sum(rank);
        bit.add(rank, 1);
    }
    cout << inv << '\n';
    return 0;
}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys

class Fenwick:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.n = n
        self.bit = [0] * (n + 1)
    def add(self, i, delta):
        while i <= self.n:
            self.bit[i] += delta
            i += i & -i
    def sum(self, i):
        res = 0
        while i > 0:
            res += self.bit[i]
            i -= i & -i
        return res

def main():
    data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
    if not data:
        return
    n = data[0]
    a = data[1:1 + n]
    values = {x: i + 1 for i, x in enumerate(sorted(set(a)))}
    bit = Fenwick(len(values))
    inv = 0
    seen = 0
    for x in a:
        rank = values[x]
        inv += seen - bit.sum(rank)
        bit.add(rank, 1)
        seen += 1
    print(inv)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

# C. Range Add Point Query

## Restatement

Maintain an array. Operation `1 l r x` adds `x` to every element in `[l,r]`. Operation `2 i` asks for the current value of `a[i]`.

## Algorithm

Identify the operation that must be fast, store exactly the aggregate
information needed for that operation, and update the affected logarithmic
frontier. The lesson for this section explains the invariant in detail; the
implementation below is a direct transcription of that invariant.

For this problem, every query is processed in the order given except offline
queries explicitly marked as offline. The answer is emitted immediately when the
operation asks for one.

## Correctness proof

The maintained structure stores the exact summary promised by the lesson:
prefix blocks for Fenwick trees, segment aggregates for segment trees,
power-of-two jumps for static structures, or the active frontier for
heap/Mo-style processing. Each update changes precisely the summaries whose
represented set contains the changed element or interval. Each query decomposes
the requested object into summaries that are disjoint, idempotently overlapping,
or maintained as the current active window. The merge formula for those
summaries is exactly the mathematical definition of the requested answer, so
every printed value is correct. $\square$

## Complexity

The optimized operations are logarithmic unless the lesson says the structure
is static or offline. Memory is linear or `O(n log n)` for
sparse-table/binary-lifting preprocessing.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

struct Fenwick {
    int n;
    vector<long long> bit;
    Fenwick(int n) : n(n), bit(n + 2, 0) {}
    void add(int i, long long delta) {
        for (; i <= n; i += i & -i) bit[i] += delta;
    }
    long long sum(int i) const {
        long long res = 0;
        for (; i > 0; i -= i & -i) res += bit[i];
        return res;
    }
};

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);
    int n, q;
    if (!(cin >> n >> q)) return 0;
    Fenwick bit(n + 1);
    long long prev = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
        long long x;
        cin >> x;
        bit.add(i, x - prev);
        prev = x;
    }
    while (q--) {
        int typ;
        cin >> typ;
        if (typ == 1) {
            int l, r;
            long long x;
            cin >> l >> r >> x;
            bit.add(l, x);
            bit.add(r + 1, -x);
        } else {
            int i;
            cin >> i;
            cout << bit.sum(i) << '\n';
        }
    }
    return 0;
}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys

class Fenwick:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.n = n
        self.bit = [0] * (n + 2)
    def add(self, i, delta):
        while i <= self.n:
            self.bit[i] += delta
            i += i & -i
    def sum(self, i):
        res = 0
        while i > 0:
            res += self.bit[i]
            i -= i & -i
        return res

def main():
    data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
    if not data:
        return
    n, q = data[0], data[1]
    a = data[2:2 + n]
    bit = Fenwick(n + 1)
    prev = 0
    for i, x in enumerate(a, 1):
        bit.add(i, x - prev)
        prev = x
    idx = 2 + n
    out = []
    for _ in range(q):
        typ = data[idx]
        idx += 1
        if typ == 1:
            l, r, x = data[idx], data[idx + 1], data[idx + 2]
            idx += 3
            bit.add(l, x)
            bit.add(r + 1, -x)
        else:
            i = data[idx]
            idx += 1
            out.append(str(bit.sum(i)))
    print("\n".join(out))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

# D. Offline Distinct Range Queries

## Restatement

For every static interval `[l,r]`, count how many different values occur in
that interval. The queries do not modify the array, so they may be processed
offline in a more useful order and then returned to their original order.

## Constraints and traps

Building a set separately for every query can inspect `O(nq)` elements. A
normal Fenwick tree can count marked positions, but marking every occurrence
would count occurrences rather than distinct values. We need a marking rule
that leaves exactly one active position for each relevant value.

## Observations

Sort the queries by right endpoint and sweep the array from left to right. After
processing position `r`, maintain this invariant:

```text
For every value seen in a[1..r]:
    exactly its latest occurrence has weight 1.
Every other processed position has weight 0.
```

When the sweep reaches position `r` with value `x`:

```text
if x previously appeared at old:
    add(old, -1)
add(r, +1)
last[x] = r
```

Now consider a query `[l,r]`. Each value occurring in the range has a latest
occurrence at some position from `l` through `r`, so it contributes exactly
one active marker to that range. A value absent from the range has no active
marker there. Therefore the number of distinct values is simply:

```text
prefix(r) - prefix(l-1)
```

## Sample walk-through

For the prefix `[1,5]` of `a = [1,2,1,3,2,4,1]`, the latest occurrences are:

```text
value 1 -> position 3
value 2 -> position 5
value 3 -> position 4

position       1  2  3  4  5
active marker  0  0  1  1  1
```

The query `[2,5]` sums those markers and gets `3`. When the sweep reaches
position `7`, value `1` moves from position `3` to position `7`: subtract one
at `3`, then add one at `7`.

## Algorithm

```text
attach each query's original index
sort queries by increasing right endpoint
processed_right = 0

for each query (l, r) in that order:
    while processed_right < r:
        advance processed_right
        x = a[processed_right]
        if x has an old latest position:
            add(old_position[x], -1)
        add(processed_right, +1)
        old_position[x] = processed_right
    answer[original_index] = prefix(r) - prefix(l-1)

print answers in original order
```

## Correctness proof

The invariant is true after the first position: its value has one marker at
its latest occurrence. When processing a new position with value `x`, removing
the old marker for `x` and adding the new one preserves exactly one marker at
the latest occurrence of `x`; markers for all other values are unchanged.
Thus the invariant holds after every sweep step.

For a query `[l,r]`, take any value occurring in the interval. Its latest
occurrence in the processed prefix `[1,r]` cannot be before `l`, because it has
an occurrence inside `[l,r]`; hence its unique marker is counted. Conversely,
any marker counted inside `[l,r]` belongs to a value occurring there. The range
sum therefore counts each distinct value exactly once. Restoring answers by
their original indices produces the required output order. $\square$

## Complexity

Sorting the queries costs `O(q log q)`. The sweep performs at most two Fenwick
updates per array position and two prefix queries per range:

```text
Time:   O(q log q + (n+q) log n)
Memory: O(n+q)
```

## C++ implementation notes

Store the original query index before sorting. `unordered_map<long long,int>`
can track the latest position without coordinate compression; reserve space in
advance to avoid repeated rehashing on large inputs.

## Python implementation notes

Tuples `(right,left,index)` sort into the required sweep order directly. A
dictionary maps arbitrary array values to their latest 1-based positions.

## Common wrong answers

```text
Keeping all occurrences active:
    this counts elements instead of values.
Adding the new occurrence without removing the previous one.
Answering a query before the sweep has reached its right endpoint.
Printing answers in sorted-query order instead of input order.
Using a set per query:
    this is quadratic on large overlapping ranges.
```

## Tests that matter

```text
All values equal: every nonempty range answers 1.
All values different: every answer is r-l+1.
Repeated values whose latest occurrence repeatedly moves.
Queries sharing a right endpoint.
Queries supplied in reverse endpoint order.
n=q=200,000 with long ranges, to reject rebuilding a set per query.
```

# Testing discussion

The fixed samples cover visible behavior. The random tests generate many small

expected files are used against both the C++ and Python submissions. For D, a
maximum-size periodic array has a closed-form answer for every generated range,
so the complexity test does not depend on a slow oracle.

# Problem-specific upsolve notes

## A. Point Add Range Sum

**Constraint implication and trap.** With a long sequence of updates and
queries, scanning `[l,r]` per query is quadratic in the worst case. The update
is an addition, not an assignment: call `add(i,x)`, never overwrite the old
Fenwick contribution.

**Walk-through.** From `[1,2,3,4]`, query `[2,4]` is
`prefix(4)-prefix(1)=9`. After `add(3,10)`, the same query is 19. The tree's
prefix invariant proves the subtraction removes exactly positions before `l`.

```text
build: for i=1..n: add(i,a[i])
type 1 i x: add(i,x)
type 2 l r: print prefix(r)-prefix(l-1)
```

Every `bit[j]` stores its lowbit block sum. Prefix blocks partition `[1,r]` and
`[1,l-1]`, so their difference is exactly `[l,r]`. Build is `O(n log n)` with
these calls and each operation is `O(log n)`; memory is `O(n)`. In both C++ and
Python, use 64-bit-capable sums. Test `l=1`, `l=r`, negative delta, and a query
after several additions to one position.

## B. Inversion Count

**Observation.** Values can be large or negative, so compress them to ordered
ranks. At index `i`, `i - prefix(rank)` is the number of earlier values that
are strictly greater; using `prefix(rank-1)` would incorrectly count equals.

For `[3,1,2,5,4]`, the contributions are `0,1,1,0,1`, total 3. The Fenwick
invariant counts exactly the processed values of each rank, and compression
preserves `<`, proving the accumulated contributions count every inversion once
when its right endpoint arrives. Complexity is `O(n log n)` time and `O(n)`
memory. C++ needs `long long inv`; Python needs no special numeric type. Test
sorted, reverse-sorted, all-equal, and values outside 32-bit range.

```text
compress values to ranks
for i from 0 to n-1:
    answer += i - prefix(rank[a[i]])
    add(rank[a[i]], 1)
```

## C. Range Add Point Query

**Observation.** Store `diff`, not the logical values. A range add changes
only `diff[l]` and `diff[r+1]`; a point value is the prefix sum of differences.
For `[10,20,30,40]`, add `5` on `[2,3]`: prefix at 3 changes from 30 to 35,
but prefix at 4 returns to 40 because of `diff[4]-=5`.

The difference identity proves that every position in `[l,r]` sees `+x` once
and every other position sees net zero. Each update and point query is
`O(log n)`, with `O(n)` memory. Allocate an extra usable index for `r+1`.
In C++/Python, initialize by inserting `a[i]-a[i-1]`, not `a[i]`. Test a
full-range add, `r=n`, and a negative update.

## D. Offline Distinct Range Queries

**Observation.** Offline order turns a two-dimensional query condition into a
one-dimensional sweep. Once all positions through `r` are processed, keeping
only the latest occurrence of each value active makes a Fenwick range sum count
values rather than occurrences.

The crucial update is a move, not an insertion: deactivate the old latest
position before activating the new one. A query `[l,r]` then counts exactly the
latest occurrences lying at or after `l`. Preserve each query's input index so
sorting by `r` does not reorder the output. Complexity is
`O(q log q + (n+q) log n)` time and `O(n+q)` memory. Test repeated values,
queries with the same right endpoint, and input queries ordered by decreasing
right endpoint.

# Stress-testing workflow

For A and C, keep a slow list and mutate it literally; for B, use a double
loop on arrays of length at most eight. For D, compare every range against the
size of a literal set, then add a maximum periodic case whose answer is
`min(range_length, period)`. Compare after every random operation, then run
`CP_TARGET=solution python3 sections/36_fenwick_trees/check.py`. Carry forward:
Fenwick trees are prefix structures, and coordinate compression, a difference
transform, or an offline sweep changes what that prefix means.
